title: Administrative and Enforcement Powers of the Government
summary: This thread covers the Government's delegated powers to appoint officers, conduct searches, impose penalties, and manage legal proceedings. These powers remain largely static in substance, reflecting the foundational enforcement mechanisms of the Customs Act 1969, which continue to be referenced in modern administrative directives.

৫। কার্য সম্পাদন জামানত (Performance Security) প্রদান।—(১) এই বিধিমালার অধীন সেবা প্রদানকারী প্রতিষ্ঠানকে কার্য সম্পাদন চুক্তি সম্পাদনের সময় ৫ (পাঁচ) কোটি টাকার কার্য সম্পাদন জামানত (Performance Security) প্রদান করিতে হইবে।
(২) উপ-বিধি (১) এ উল্লিখিত জামানত ব্যাংক গ্যারান্টি আকারে সদস্য, কাস্টমস নীতি, জাতীয় রাজস্ব বোর্ডের অনুকূলে দাখিল করিতে হইবে যাহার কার্যকারিতা সেবা প্রদানের জন্য উল্লিখিত তারিখ হইতে চুক্তির মেয়াদ শেষ হইবার তারিখের পরবর্তী ৯০ (নব্বই) দিন পর্যন্ত বহাল থাকিবে:
তবে শর্ত থাকে যে, বোর্ড কোনো নিষ্পত্তিকৃত বা অবিতর্কিত সরকারি পাওনা আদায়ের জন্য উপ-বিধি (১) এর অধীন প্রদত্ত কার্য সম্পাদন জামানত আংশিক বা সম্পূর্ণ নগদায়ন ও বাজেয়াপ্তির আদেশ প্রদান করিতে পারিবে।
(৩) কোনো সেবা প্রদানকারী প্রতিষ্ঠানের সহিত সম্পাদিত চুক্তি বাতিল করা হইলে বা কার্য সম্পাদন জামানতের মেয়াদ উত্তীর্ণ হইলে, যদি সরকারের নিকট উক্ত প্রতিষ্ঠানের কোনো দায় বা অন্য কোনো অনিষ্পন্ন দায় বা দায়িত্ব না থাকে তাহা হইলে বোর্ড সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠানের আবেদনের পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে কার্য সম্পাদন জামানত অবমুক্ত করিবে।

Security Deposit: A service provider is required to submit a performance security deposit at the time of executing the service agreement. The Board reserves the right to partially or fully encash or forfeit this deposit to recover settled or undisputed government dues.

The security deposit must be provided in the form of a bank guarantee in favor of the Member, Customs Policy, National Board of Revenue. It must remain valid from the specified start date of service until ninety days after the expiry of the agreement term.

Upon the termination of an agreement or the expiry of the security deposit, the Board shall release the deposit upon application by the service provider, provided there are no outstanding liabilities or duties owed to the government.
National Board of Revenue: The Board is empowered to encash or forfeit the performance security deposit for the recovery of undisputed government claims.
The Board is responsible for releasing the performance security deposit to the service provider after the expiry of the agreement, provided all government liabilities have been settled.
Logistics and Security Service Provider: A service provider must provide a performance security deposit when entering into a service agreement. They are eligible to apply for the release of their security deposit once the agreement ends, provided no outstanding obligations to the government exist.

(২) বিধি (১) অনুসারে উক্ত স্বীকৃতি চুক্তির আওতায় অন্য দেশের স্বীকৃতিপ্রাপ্ত caravan এর জন্য চুক্তির শর্ত মোতাবেক পারস্পরিক ভিত্তিতে অথরাইজড ইকোনমিক অপারেটর সুবিধা প্রদান ও শর্তাবলি নির্ধারণের জন্য বোর্ড আদেশ জারি করিতে পারিবে।

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is authorized to enter into mutual recognition agreements with other countries to ensure reciprocal benefits for authorized economic operators.
The board is empowered to issue orders to grant authorized economic operator benefits and define terms and conditions for entities recognized by foreign countries under these reciprocal agreements.
Authorized Economic Operator: Authorized economic operators are subject to mutual recognition agreements that allow them to receive corresponding benefits in other countries based on reciprocal arrangements.

Benefits and operational conditions for foreign-recognized authorized economic operators are determined by the National Board of Revenue through formal orders following the signing of mutual recognition agreements.
Mutual Recognition Agreement: A mutual recognition agreement is a formal treaty between the government and a foreign country designed to grant reciprocal trade facilitation benefits to authorized economic operators.
These agreements serve as the legal framework under which the National Board of Revenue can extend specific operational advantages to foreign entities recognized under the program.

Customs Station: The customs station authority is responsible for allowing authorized entities to deposit applicable duties and taxes into the government treasury based on the declarations provided in the bill of entry or bill of export.
Bill of Entry: This document serves as the basis for the declaration of imported goods and is used to determine the applicable duties and taxes payable to the government.
Bill of Export: This document is utilized for the declaration of exported goods, enabling the customs authority to assess any applicable duties and taxes before processing.
Customs Duty: The customs authorities must ensure that all applicable duties and taxes related to imported or exported goods are deposited into the government treasury by the declarant.

Customs Act 1969: This clause establishes transitional provisions for cases and proceedings that were pending under sections 193, 196, 193A, and 196B of the Act prior to a designated date.
It mandates the transfer of certain pending appeals and proceedings from the National Board of Revenue or the Government to the Customs Appellate Tribunal.
National Board of Revenue: Appeals pending before the Board under section 193 of the Customs Act 1969 are transferred to the Customs Appellate Tribunal as of the designated date.
The Board's actions regarding proceedings pending under section 193A continue to remain valid as if the relevant sections had not been replaced.
Customs Appellate Tribunal: The Tribunal assumes jurisdiction over all appeals and proceedings transferred from the Board or the Government under this transitional provision.
The Tribunal is empowered to dispose of transferred appeals or proceedings, while ensuring that the appellant or involved parties retain the right to request a fresh hearing.
Government: Proceedings pending before the Government under section 196 of the Customs Act 1969 are generally transferred to the Customs Appellate Tribunal, except for specific categories of cases involving defined monetary thresholds or commodity valuations.
For specific excepted categories, the Government retains the authority to continue proceedings as if the original legal provisions remained in force.
The Government's actions regarding proceedings pending under section 196B continue to remain valid as if the relevant sections had not been replaced.

Customs Act 1969: The Act provides the legal framework governing personal appearance and representation before customs authorities, appellate bodies, the Board, or the Government.
It sets the conditions under which persons may be represented by authorized agents during proceedings initiated under the Act or its associated rules.
Customs Authority: This entity covers customs officials, appellate authorities, the National Board of Revenue, and the Government, before whom legal proceedings under the Customs Act 1969 are conducted.
Authorized Representative: A person is entitled to be represented by an authorized person, such as a relative, a regularly employed individual, a qualified advocate, or a licensed customs consultant during customs proceedings.
Individuals dismissed from government service are explicitly prohibited from acting as authorized representatives in these proceedings.
A Commissioner of Customs has the authority to disqualify a representative found guilty of misconduct from appearing in future customs proceedings.
National Board of Revenue: The Board acts as the appellate body for individuals wishing to contest an order issued by a Commissioner of Customs that disqualifies them from acting as a representative.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner is empowered to investigate professional misconduct by customs consultants or other representatives and issue orders declaring them unfit to represent parties in customs proceedings.
The Commissioner must provide a reasonable opportunity for a hearing before issuing any order of disqualification against a representative.

The Act is designed to become effective on a date determined and publicly announced by the Government through an official gazette notification.
Government: The Government is granted the legal authority to determine and announce the specific commencement date for the enforcement of the Act through an official gazette notification.

member_objects.clause_title: Clearance of warehoused goods for export
member_objects.resolved_text:
105. Clearance of warehoused goods for export.- Any owner of warehoused goods may, at any time within the period of their warehousing under section 98, clear such goods for export out of 2[Bangladesh] on payment of all rent, penalties, interest and other charges payable as aforesaid but without paying any import duty thereon:
Provide that, if the 3[Government] is of the opinion that warehoused goods of any specified description are likely to be smuggled back into 2[Bangladesh], it may, by notification in the official Gazette, direct that such goods shall not be exported to any place outside 2[Bangladesh] without payment of duty or allow them to be exported subject to such restrictions and conditions as may be specified in the notification.

Owner of Warehoused Goods: The owner of warehoused goods is permitted to clear their goods for export at any time during the authorized warehousing period.
Export clearance is conditional upon the full payment of all relevant rent, interest, penalties, and associated charges.
Warehoused Goods: These goods may be cleared for export without the payment of import duty.
The government reserves the right to restrict the export of specific goods if there is a risk that they may be smuggled back into the country.
The government may mandate the payment of duty or impose specific conditions and restrictions on the export of certain warehoused goods via an official notification.
Government: The government has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to restrict the export of certain goods if it determines that such goods are prone to being smuggled back into the country.

member_objects.clause_title: Power to prohibit or restrict importation and exportation of goods
member_objects.resolved_text: 16. Power to prohibit or restrict importation and exportation of goods.- The 2[Government] may, from time to time, by notification in the official Gazette, prohibit or restrict the bringing into or taking out of 3[Bangladesh] of any goods of specified description by air, sea or land.

Government: The Government is empowered to issue notifications in the official Gazette to prohibit or restrict the import or export of specific types of goods.
Importation: The Government has the legal authority to restrict or prohibit the bringing of specific goods into Bangladesh by air, sea, or land.
Export: The Government has the legal authority to restrict or prohibit the taking of specific goods out of Bangladesh by air, sea, or land.
Goods: The Government may regulate the movement of goods into or out of the country by issuing notifications that specify descriptions of goods subject to prohibition or restriction.

member_objects.clause_title: Application of certain provisions of this Act to coastal goods
member_objects.resolved_text:
154. Application of certain provisions of this Act to coastal goods.- (1) Sections 64, 65 and 66 shall, so far as may be, apply to coastal goods as they apply to imported goods or goods for export.
(2) Section 48 and 60 shall, so far as may be, apply to vessels carrying coastal goods as they apply to vessels carrying imported goods or goods for export.
(3) The 1[Government] may, by notification in the official Gazette, direct that all or any of the other provisions of Chapter VII and the provisions of section 78 shall apply to coastal goods or vessels carrying coastal goods with such exceptions and modifications, if any, as may be specified in the notification.

Coastal Goods: The provisions of the Act relating to imported or exported goods, specifically sections 64, 65, and 66, are extended to apply to coastal goods. The Government may also extend additional provisions from Chapter VII and section 78 to these goods, subject to any exceptions or modifications specified in a notification.
Vessels Carrying Coastal Goods: The provisions of the Act governing vessels that carry imported or exported goods, specifically sections 48 and 60, are extended to apply to vessels carrying coastal goods. The Government has the authority to apply further regulatory provisions of the Act to these vessels through an official gazette notification.
Government: The Government is empowered to issue official notifications to extend specific provisions of Chapter VII and section 78 of the Act to coastal goods or vessels carrying coastal goods, potentially including specific modifications or exceptions.

member_objects.clause_title: Power to search on reasonable ground
member_objects.resolved_text:
158. Power to search on reasonable ground.- (1) The appropriate officer, if he has reason to believe that any person is carrying about himself goods liable to confiscation or any documents relating thereto, may search such person, if he has landed from or is on board or is about to board a vessel within the 3[Bangladesh] customs-waters, or if he has alighted from or is about to get into or is in any other conveyance arriving in or proceeding from 3[Bangladesh] or if he is entering or about to leave 3[Bangladesh] or if he is within the limits of any customs-area.
(2) Without prejudice to the provisions of sub-section (1) the appropriate officer may search a person, if he has reason to believe that such person is carrying about himself smuggled Platinum, any radio active mineral, gold, silver, precious stones, manufactures of Platinum, any radio active mineral, gold, silver or precious stones, or currency, or any other goods or class of goods notified by the 4[Government] in the official Gazette, or any documents relating to any one or more of the aforementioned goods.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to search any person if there is a reasonable belief that the individual is carrying goods liable to confiscation or related documents.
The officer may conduct searches on persons located within customs-areas, in conveyances, or on vessels within Bangladesh customs-waters.
The officer has the authority to search persons suspected of carrying specific prohibited items like gold, silver, currency, or precious stones, or other goods notified by the Government.
Person: A person is subject to search by an appropriate officer if they are suspected of carrying goods liable to confiscation while present in customs-areas, or upon boarding or leaving vessels and conveyances.
Vessel: Vessels within the Bangladesh customs-waters serve as specific locations where an appropriate officer may exercise search powers over persons on board.
Conveyance: The appropriate officer is authorized to search persons arriving in or departing from Bangladesh who are in, alighting from, or entering into any conveyance.
Bangladesh customs-waters: This geographic area defines a zone where an appropriate officer may board and search vessels and the individuals located thereon.
Customs-area: The limits of a customs-area constitute a jurisdictional boundary within which the appropriate officer is granted the power to search persons.
Smuggled Goods: The search powers extend to persons suspected of carrying precious metals, minerals, stones, or currency, as well as any other goods specifically notified by the Government in the official Gazette.
Government: The Government has the authority to notify in the official Gazette specific classes of goods that, when carried by a person, provide grounds for a search by the appropriate officer.

member_objects.clause_title: Conferring certain Powers of Magistrate 1st Class on Customs officers
member_objects.resolved_text: 5[158A. Conferring certain Powers of Magistrate 1st Class on Customs officers.- For the purposes of entry search, seizure and arrest under this Act, the Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, confer the powers of a Magistrate of the First Class described in the Schedule III of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898) on an officer of customs not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner.]

Customs Officer: The Government is empowered to grant specific powers of a Magistrate of the First Class to officers of customs holding the rank of Assistant Commissioner or higher.
These conferred powers are limited to the purposes of conducting entry, search, seizure, and arrest as provided under the Customs Act 1969.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: This Act serves as the legal reference for the powers of a Magistrate of the First Class that can be conferred upon authorized customs officials under the customs law.
Government: The Government has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to formally grant magisterial powers to designated customs officials.

member_objects.clause_title: Power to screen or X-Ray bodies of suspected persons for detecting secreted goods
member_objects.resolved_text:
160. Power to screen or X-Ray bodies of suspected persons for detecting secreted goods.- (1) Where the appropriate officer has reason to believe that any person liable to search under section 158 has any goods liable to confiscation secreted inside his body, he may detain such person and produce him without unnecessary delay before an officer of customs not below the rank of an 2[Assistant Commissioner of Customs].
(2) The aforesaid officer, if he has reasonable grounds for believing that such person has any such goods secreted inside his body and that it is necessary to have the body of such person screened or X-Rayed, may make an order to that effect, or else discharge such person forthwith, except where he is held on any other grounds.
(3) Where the aforesaid officer orders such person to be screened or X-Rayed, the appropriate officer shall, as soon as practicable, take him to a radiologist possessing such qualifications as may be recognised by the 3[Government] for that purpose and such person shall allow the radiologist to screen or X-Ray his body.
(4) The radiologist shall screen or X-Ray the body of such person and forward his report thereon, together with any X-Ray pictures taken by him to the aforesaid officer without unnecessary delay.
(5) Where on the basis of a report from a radiologist or otherwise, the aforesaid officer is satisfied that any person has any goods liable to confiscation secreted inside his body , he may direct that suitable action for bringing such goods out of his body be taken on the advice and under the supervision of a registered medical practitioner and such person shall be bound to comply with such direction:
Provided that in the case of a female no such action shall be taken except on the advice and under the supervision of a female registered medical practitioner.
(6) Where any person is brought before an officer of customs not below the rank of an 1[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] as aforesaid, he may direct that pending completion of all action under this section such person be detained.
(7) No person shall be subjected to screening or X-Ray if he confesses that goods liable to confiscation are secreted inside his body and of his own consent agrees to suitable steps being taken to bring out such goods.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer is authorized to detain a suspected person if there is reason to believe they have secreted goods inside their body that are liable to confiscation.
The officer must promptly produce the detained person before an officer of at least the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs for further authorization of screening or X-ray procedures.
The officer is responsible for taking the suspect to a recognized radiologist for screening and must supervise or direct the removal of any secreted goods based on medical advice.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: A customs officer at or above the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs is authorized to review the case of a detained person and order a body screening or X-ray if reasonable grounds exist.
This officer is empowered to direct the detention of a suspect while the required medical actions or investigations are being completed.
Confiscated Goods: Goods suspected of being secreted inside a person's body and which are liable to confiscation are subject to detection through screening or X-ray procedures.
The law provides mechanisms for the recovery of such goods under medical supervision when their presence is confirmed.
Radiologist: A radiologist, possessing qualifications recognized by the Government, is the authorized professional tasked with performing body screenings or X-rays on suspects to detect secreted goods.
The radiologist is required to forward the screening report and any associated imagery to the relevant customs officer without delay.
Registered Medical Practitioner: Any action taken to remove secreted goods from a person's body must be performed under the advice and supervision of a registered medical practitioner.
In the case of a female suspect, the intervention must be supervised specifically by a female registered medical practitioner.
Government: The Government is responsible for recognizing the qualifications of the radiologists authorized to perform the medical procedures required for detecting secreted goods.

member_objects.clause_title: Power to search and arrest without warrant
member_objects.resolved_text:
163. Power to search and arrest without warrant.- (1) Whenever any officer or customs not below the rank of an 1[Assistant Commissioner of Customs] or any other officer 2[* * * *] employed for the prevention of smuggling has reasonable grounds for believing that any goods liable to confiscation or any documents or things which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to any proceeding under this Act are concealed or kept in any place and that there is a danger that they may be removed before a search can be effected under section 162, he may, after preparing a statement in writing of the grounds of his belief and of the goods, documents or things for which search is to be made, search or cause of search to be made for such goods, documents or things in that place.
(2) Any officer or person who makes a search or causes a search to be made under sub-section (1) shall leave a signed copy of the aforementioned statement in or about the place searched and shall, at the time the search is made or as soon as is practicable thereafter, deliver furthermore a signed copy of such statement to the occupier of the place at his last known address.
(3) All searches made under this section shall be carried out mutatis mutandis in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898).
(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing sub-sections and subject to previous authorization by an officer of customs not below the rank of an 1[Assistant Commissioner of Customs], any officer of customs or any person duly empowered as such may, with respect to an offence 3[of smuggling]-
(a) arrest without warrant any person concerned in such offence or against whom reasonable suspicion exists that he is about to be concerned in such offence;
(b) enter and search without warrant any premises to make an arrest under clause (a), or to seize an goods which are reasonable suspected to be intended for 4[smuggling] contrary to any prohibition or restriction for the time being in force, and all documents or things which in his opinion will be useful for or relevant to any proceeding under this Act; and
(c) for the purpose of arresting, detaining or taking into custody or preventing the escape of any person concerned or likely to be concerned in such offence, or for the purpose of seizing or preventing the removal of any goods in respect of which any such offence has occurred or is likely to occur, use or cause to be used such force to the extent of causing death as may be necessary.
(5) The provisions of sub-section (4) shall apply only to the areas within five miles of the land frontier of 1[Bangladesh], and within a five mile belt running along the sea coast of 1[Bangladesh].
(6) No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall be instituted, except with the previous sanction in writing of the 2[Government], against any person in respect of anything done or purporting to be done in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) or, in the areas specified in sub-section (3), by sub-section (4).

Assistant Commissioner of Customs: This officer is authorized to form beliefs regarding the concealment of goods or documents subject to search and to authorize officers to conduct searches or arrests without a warrant under specified conditions.
Smuggling: The prevention of smuggling is a primary function that empowers customs officers to carry out searches and arrests without a warrant in defined circumstances.
Specific enforcement powers, including the use of force and warrantless entry of premises, are granted to customs officers when dealing with offences related to smuggling.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: All searches conducted under this section must adhere to the procedural requirements established in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
Officer of Customs: Officers are empowered to enter and search premises, seize goods suspected of smuggling, and arrest individuals involved in such offences without a warrant under specific conditions.
When necessary to execute duties such as arresting persons or seizing goods, these officers may use force, including lethal force, to prevent escape or the removal of illicit items.
Government: Legal proceedings cannot be instituted against any person acting under the powers granted in this section without the prior written sanction of the Government.
Customs Offence: Special enforcement provisions apply to offences related to smuggling, allowing for warrantless arrests, entry of premises, and the use of force within designated border and coastal zones.

member_objects.clause_title: Power to stop and search conveyances
member_objects.resolved_text:
164. Power to stop and search conveyances.- (1) Where the appropriate officer has reason to believe that within the territories of 1[Bangladesh] (including territorial waters) any conveyance has been, is being, or is about to be used in the smuggling of any goods or in the carriage of any smuggled goods, he may at any time stop any such conveyance or, in the case of an aircraft, competent it to land, and-
(a) rummage and search any part of the conveyance ;
(b) examine and search any goods thereon ; and
(c) break open the lock f any door, fixure or package for making search.
(2) Where in the circumstances referred to in sub-section (1)-
(a) it becomes necessary to stop any vessel or compel any aircraft to land, it shall be lawful for any vessel or aircraft in the service of the Government while flying her proper flag or bearing flag marks and any authority authorised in this behalf by the 3[Government] to summon such vessel to stop or the aircraft to land, by means of an international signal, code or other recognised means, and thereupon such vessel shall forthwith stop or such aircraft shall forthwith land, and it fails to do so, chase may be given there to by any vessel or aircraft as aforesaid and if after a gun is fired as a signal the vessel fails to stop or the aircraft fails to land, it may be fired upon;
(b) it becomes necessary to stop any conveyance other than a vessel or aircraft, the appropriate officer may use or cause to be used all lawful means for stopping it or preventing it escape including, if all other means fail, firing upon it.

Appropriate Officer of Customs: This officer is empowered to stop and search any conveyance if they have reason to believe it is being used for smuggling goods or transporting smuggled goods within Bangladesh.
They are authorized to search, examine, and break open any locks, fixtures, or packages within the conveyance to carry out these duties.
When dealing with conveyances other than vessels or aircraft, they may use all lawful means to stop or prevent the escape of the conveyance, including firing upon it as a last resort.
Conveyance: Any conveyance, including vessels and aircraft, suspected of involvement in smuggling or carrying smuggled goods is subject to being stopped, searched, or compelled to land by customs authorities.
Owners or operators are legally required to stop immediately when signaled by authorized government vessels or aircraft, or face the risk of being chased or fired upon if they fail to comply.
Smuggling: This act forms the basis for the enforcement powers granted to customs officers to intervene against vehicles or vessels suspected of facilitating the illegal movement of goods.
Smuggled Goods: The transport of such goods within Bangladesh grants customs officers the legal authority to intercept and search any conveyance found to be carrying or intending to carry them.
Government: The government is authorized to designate specific authorities to signal vessels or aircraft to stop or land, and may employ government vessels or aircraft to enforce these directives through international signaling or the use of force.

member_objects.clause_title: Power to detain packages containing certain publications imported in [Bangladesh]
member_objects.resolved_text:
172. Power to detain packages containing certain publications imported in 2[Bangladesh].- (1) Any officer of customs duly authorised by the 3[Commissioner of Customs] or any other officer authorised by the 4[Government] in this behalf may detain any package, brought whether by land, air or sea into 2[Bangladesh] which he suspects to contain-
5[(a) any newspaper or book as defined in the Printing Presses and Publications (Declaration and Registration) Act, 1973 (XXIII of 1973), or]
(b) any document, containing any treasonable or seditious matter, that is to say, any matter, the publication of which is punishable under section 123A or section 124A, as the case may be, of the 6[Penal Code] (Act XLV of 1860), and shall forward such package to such officer as the 4[Government] may appoint in this behalf.
(2) Any officer detaining a package under sub-section (1) shall, where practicable, forthwith send by post to the addressee or consignee of such package notice of the fact of such detention.
(3) The 4[Government] shall cause the contents of such package to be examined, and if it appears to the 4[Government] that the package contains any such newspaper, book or other document, as aforesaid, it may pass such order as to the disposal of the package and its contents as it may deem proper, and, if it does not so appear, shall release the package and its contents unless the same be otherwise liable to seizure under any law for the time being in force:
Provided that any person interested in any package detained under the provisions of this section, may, within two months of the date of such detention, apply to the 4[Government] for release of the same, and the 4[Government] shall consider such application and pass such order thereon as it may deem to be proper:
Provided further that, if such application is rejected, the applicant may, within two months of the date of the order rejecting the application, apply to the 1[High Court Division] for release of the package or its contents on the ground that the package or the contents do not contain any such newspaper, book or other document.
(4) No order passed or action taken under this section shall be called in question in any court save as provided in the second proviso to sub-section (3).
Explanation.- In this section "document" includes any writing, painting, engraving, drawing or photograph or other visible representation.

Officer of Customs: Officers duly authorized by the Commissioner of Customs or the Government are empowered to detain packages imported into Bangladesh that are suspected to contain prohibited publications or seditious materials.
An officer who detains a package must, where practicable, provide notification of the detention to the addressee or consignee.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs is authorized to grant the power to specific officers to detain packages suspected of containing prohibited materials.
Government: The Government is empowered to appoint specific officers to receive detained packages for further examination.
The Government has the authority to examine the contents of detained packages and pass orders regarding their disposal or release.
The Government acts as the deciding authority for applications regarding the release of detained packages, with decisions being subject to review by the High Court Division under specific conditions.
Detained Goods: Packages containing prohibited newspapers, books, or documents are subject to detention and subsequent inspection by the Government.

Any person with an interest in a detained package may apply to the Government for its release within a specified timeframe, or subsequently appeal to the High Court Division if the application is rejected.
Printing Presses and Publications (Decla: This Act provides the definitions for newspapers and books that may be subject to detention if imported into Bangladesh.
Penal Code 1860: Packages containing documents with treasonable or seditious matter, as defined by specific sections of the Penal Code 1860, are liable for detention and examination.
High Court Division: The High Court Division serves as the appellate authority for individuals seeking the release of detained packages after their initial application to the Government has been rejected.

member_objects.clause_title: Restriction or the possession of goods in certain areas
member_objects.resolved_text:
177. Restriction or the possession of goods in certain areas.- (1) This section shall apply to such areas adjacent to the frontier of 1[Bangladesh] as may, from time to time, be notified by the Board in the official Gazette.
2[(2) In any area to which this section for the time being applies, no person shall have in his possession or control any such goods or class of goods in excess of such quantity or value as may from time to time be notified by the Government in the official Gazette, except under a permit granted by the Government in respect of the particular goods or class of goods, or by an officer authorised by the Government.]

Goods: The possession or control of specific goods or classes of goods within designated frontier areas is restricted.
Possession of such goods in excess of a notified quantity or value is prohibited unless authorized by a permit issued by the Government or an authorized officer.
National Board of Revenue: The Board has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to designate specific areas adjacent to the frontier where these restrictions on goods apply.
Government: The Government is empowered to notify the maximum quantity or value of specific goods that may be held within restricted frontier areas.
The Government or its authorized officers maintain the authority to issue permits allowing for the possession of restricted goods in excess of the defined limits.

member_objects.clause_title: Vesting of confiscated property in the [Government]
member_objects.resolved_text: 182. Vesting of confiscated property in the 4[Government].- When any goods are confiscated under this Act they shall forthwith vest in the 4[Government], and the officer who orders confiscation shall take and hold possession of the confiscated goods.

Government: Confiscated goods vest automatically and immediately in the Government upon the issuance of a confiscation order under the Act.
Confiscated Goods: Once goods are subject to an order of confiscation, they legally belong to the Government.
The customs officer who issues the confiscation order is responsible for taking and maintaining physical possession of the confiscated items.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal authority for the confiscation of goods and establishes the procedures for the transfer of ownership to the Government.

member_objects.clause_title: Special power for Magistrates
member_objects.resolved_text: 185. Special power for Magistrates.- Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 ( Act V of 1898 ) and subject to the other provisions of this Act, any Magistrate of the first class specially empowered by the 2[Government] in this behalf may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term exceeding 3[five years] and of fine exceeding 4[ten thousand taka] for an offence under this Act.

Magistrate: A Magistrate of the first class who is specially empowered by the Government is granted the authority to impose sentences of imprisonment and fines exceeding statutory limits for offences committed under the Customs Act 1969.
This special power granted to the Magistrate operates notwithstanding the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, but remains subject to other provisions of the Customs Act 1969.
Code of Criminal Procedure 1898: The sentencing powers granted to a specially empowered Magistrate under the Customs Act 1969 are exercised notwithstanding the general limitations prescribed in this Code.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal framework for the prosecution of customs offences and empowers the Government to designate Magistrates with enhanced sentencing authority.
The exercise of special sentencing powers by a Magistrate remains subject to the provisions contained within this Act.
Government: The Government is empowered to specially authorize a Magistrate of the first class to exercise enhanced sentencing powers for offences committed under the Customs Act 1969.

member_objects.clause_title: Notice of conviction to be displayed
member_objects.resolved_text:
189. Notice of conviction to be displayed.- (1) Upon the conviction of any person for the offence of smuggling, the 1[Government] may require him to exhibit in or outside, or both in and outside, his place of business, if any notices of such number, size and lettering, and placed in such positions and containing such particulars relating to the conviction as it may determine, and to keep them so exhibited continuously for a period not less than three months from the date of conviction; and if he fails to comply fully with the requirement he shall be deemed to have committed a further offence under this Act of the nature of the original offence for which he was convicted.
(2) If any person so convicted refuses or fails to comply fully with any such requirement, any officer authorised in that behalf by an order of the 1[Government] in writing may, without prejudice to any proceedings which may be brought in respect of any such refusal or failure, affix the notices in or outside, or both in or outside, the place of business of such person in accordance with the requirement of the 1[Government] in pursuance of sub-section (1).
(3) If, in any case the 1[Government] is satisfied that the exhibition of notices in accordance with the requirements of the provisions of sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) will not effectively bring the conviction to the notice of persons dealing with the convicted person, the 1[Government] may, in lieu of, or in addition to any such requirement, require the convicted person to exhibit for such period, not being a period less than three months, on such stationery used in his business as may be specified in the requirement; and, if he fails to comply fully with the requirement, he shall be deemed to have committed a further offence under this Act of the nature of the original offence for which he was convicted.

Smuggling: A person convicted of smuggling may be legally required to publicly display notices of their conviction at their place of business for a mandatory minimum period.
Failure to comply with the display requirements for conviction notices constitutes a further offence of the same nature as the original smuggling offence.
Government: The Government is empowered to determine the specifications of conviction notices, including their size, lettering, number, and placement.

The Government may authorize officers to enter and affix such notices if the convicted person fails to comply with the requirement, and it may also mandate that notices be printed on business stationery if public display is deemed ineffective.
Person: A person convicted of a smuggling offence faces additional legal obligations, including the mandated display of their conviction to the public or their business contacts.
Failure to adhere to these display mandates results in the person being deemed to have committed a fresh offence equivalent to the original smuggling conviction.
Officer of Customs: An officer authorized by the Government may, in the event of a convicted person's refusal or failure, enter the person's place of business to affix the required conviction notices on their behalf.

member_objects.clause_title: Power to publish conviction
member_objects.resolved_text: 190. Power to publish conviction.- If the 1[Government] is satisfied that it is necessary so to do, the conviction and the particulars relating to the conviction of any person for the offence of smuggling may be published in the official Gazette.

Government: The Government is empowered to publish the details of a person's conviction for smuggling in the official Gazette when it deems such publication necessary.
Smuggling Offences: The Government has the authority to release information regarding the conviction and specific particulars of any person found guilty of smuggling through the official Gazette.

member_objects.clause_title: Effects of Agreement or Resolution
member_objects.resolved_text:
192 I. Effects of Agreement or Resolution .- (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of this Act where an agreement is concluded for ADR under this chapter, it shall be binding for both the parties and cannot be challenged in any appellate forum or court either by the applicant or by the customs authorities.
(2) Every order of agreement, passed under this chapter shall be conclusive as to the matters stated therein and no matter covered by such order shall, save as otherwise provided in this chapter, be reopened in any proceeding under this Act or under any other law for the time being in force.
(3) If the dues, payable to either party as per agreement, are not paid and if the same including any penalty or interest for default in making payment of such sum, if not paid within one year, such sum may either be recovered or refunded with annually 10 percent interest, or as sums due to the Government under section 202 or the applicant under section 33 of this Act.

Alternative Dispute Resolution: Once an agreement is reached under this mechanism, it becomes legally binding on both the applicant and the customs authorities.

An agreement reached through this process cannot be challenged in any court or appellate forum, and matters covered by the agreement are considered conclusive and cannot be reopened in subsequent legal proceedings.
Duty Payment: If dues resulting from an agreement are not paid, they may be recovered or refunded with an annual interest rate, and such sums are treated as amounts due to the Government or the applicant under the relevant provisions of the Customs Act 1969.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the overarching legal framework for Alternative Dispute Resolution and establishes the procedures for recovering or refunding payments and interest due under such agreements.

member_objects.clause_title: Review Committee
member_objects.resolved_text:
2[3[193C, Review Committee.- 4[(1) There shall be a Review Committee consisting of such number of members as the Board may determine for the purposes of reviewing any matter related to the Clean Report of Findings (CRF) issued by the pre-shipment inspection agencies appointed by the Government under section 25A.]
(2) Any person aggrieved by any decision of the Review Committee may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 196.
(3) The Appellate Tribunal may, after making such enquiry as it considers necessary and after giving the Commissioner or his authorised representative, the local representative of the concerned pre-shipment inspection agency, and the importer an opportunity of being heard, if they so desire, pass such order as it thinks fit, including fixing the price of the subject goods for the purpose of final assessment.
(4) No fee shall be payable for an appeal under this section.]

Review Committee: A Review Committee is established with a number of members determined by the National Board of Revenue to review matters concerning Clean Report of Findings issued by pre-shipment inspection agencies.
Any person who is aggrieved by a decision of this committee is entitled to file an appeal with the Appellate Tribunal.
National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is authorized to determine the number of members to serve on the Review Committee.
Pre-shipment Inspection Agency: These agencies are appointed by the Government under the Customs Act to issue Clean Report of Findings, which are subject to review by the Review Committee.
Local representatives of these agencies must be provided an opportunity to be heard by the Appellate Tribunal during appeal proceedings.
Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: The Appellate Tribunal is authorized to hear appeals against decisions made by the Review Committee.

The Tribunal is empowered to conduct inquiries and pass final orders, including determining the value of goods for final assessment, after providing a hearing to the Commissioner of Customs, the pre-shipment inspection agency, and the importer.
No fees are required to be paid for filing an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal under this section.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs or their authorized representative is entitled to be heard by the Appellate Tribunal during the appeal process regarding the Review Committee's decision.
Importer: The importer has the right to be heard by the Appellate Tribunal during proceedings related to the review of findings issued by pre-shipment inspection agencies.

member_objects.clause_title: Sums due to be paid notwithstanding reference, etc.
member_objects.resolved_text: 3[196H. Sums due to be paid notwithstanding reference, etc.- Notwithstanding that a reference has been made to the High Court Division, sums due to the Government as a result of an order passed under sub-section (1) of section 196B shall be payable in accordance with the order so passed.]

Government: Sums payable to the Government following a specific legal order must be paid regardless of whether an appeal or reference has been filed with the High Court Division.
High Court Division: The initiation of a reference case before the High Court Division does not stay the requirement to pay sums due under an order issued by customs authorities.

member_objects.clause_title: Transfer of certain pending proceedings and transitional provisions
member_objects.resolved_text:
5[196J. Transfer of certain pending proceedings and transitional provisions.- (1) Every appeal which is pending immediately before the appointed day before the Board under section 193 as it stood immediately before that day, and any matter arising out of or connected with such appeal and which is so pending shall stand transferred on that day to the Appellate Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal may proceed with such appeal or matter from the stage at which it was on that day:
Provided that the appellant may demand that before proceeding further with that appeal or matter, he may be re-heard.
(2) Every proceeding which is pending immediately before the appointed day before the Government under section 196 as it stood immediately before that day, and any matter arising out of or connected with such proceeding and which is so pending shall stand transferred on that day to the Appellate Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal may proceed with such proceeding or matter from the stage at which it was on that day as if such proceeding or matter were an appeal filed before it:
Provided that if any such proceeding or matter relates to an order where-
(a) the value of the goods confiscated without option having been given to the owner of the goods to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation under section 181(1); or
(b) in any disputed case, other than a case where the determination of any question having a relation to the rate of duty of customs or to the value of goods for purposes of assessment is in issue or is one of the points in issue, the difference in duty involved or the duty involved; or
(c) the amount of fine or penalty determined by such order;
does not exceed ten thousand taka such proceeding or matter shall continue to be dealt with by the Government as if the said section 196 had not been substituted:
Provided further that the applicant or the other party may make a demand to the Appellate Tribunal that before proceeding further with that proceeding or matter, he may be re-heard.
(3) Every proceeding which is pending immediately before the appointed day before the Board under section 193A or before the Government under section 196B as they stood immediately before that day, and any matter arising out of or connected with such proceeding and which is so pending shall continue to be dealt with by the Board or the Government, as the case may be, as if the said sections had not been substituted.
(4) Any person who immediately before the appointed day was authorised to appear in any appeal or proceeding transferred under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall, notwithstanding anything contained in section 196K, have the right to appear before the Appellate Tribunal in relation to such appeal or proceeding.]

Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribun: The Appellate Tribunal is designated as the successor body for the transfer of pending appeals and proceedings that were previously under the jurisdiction of the Board or the Government before the appointed day.
The Appellate Tribunal is empowered to continue proceedings from the stage they reached prior to the transfer and must allow for re-hearing upon the request of an appellant or party involved.
National Board of Revenue: Pending appeals previously filed before the Board under the former provisions are transferred to the Appellate Tribunal, while other specific pending proceedings continue to be handled by the Board as if the relevant sections had not been substituted.
Government: The Government retains jurisdiction over certain pending proceedings related to customs orders where the value of confiscated goods, the difference in duty, or the penalty amount does not exceed a specified threshold.
Proceedings not meeting the criteria for transfer to the Appellate Tribunal continue to be processed by the Government as if the original legal provisions remained in effect.
Confiscation of Goods: For cases involving goods confiscated without an option for a fine in lieu of confiscation, the value of the goods determines whether the legal proceeding is transferred to the Appellate Tribunal or remains under the authority of the Government.
Customs Duty Rate: Cases involving the determination of customs duty rates or the value of goods for assessment purposes are excluded from the threshold-based retention of jurisdiction by the Government.
Customs Legal Proceedings: The act provides transitional mechanisms for pending legal matters, establishing clear rules for the transfer of cases to the Appellate Tribunal while ensuring the right of parties to seek re-hearing.
Legal practitioners or authorized representatives who were active in proceedings prior to the transition retain their right to appear before the Appellate Tribunal for the transferred cases.

member_objects.clause_title: Appearance by the authorised representative
member_objects.resolved_text:
1[2[196K]. Appearance by the authorised representative.- Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, any person, who is entitled or required to attend before any officer of customs, an appellate authority, the Board or the Government in any proceedings under this Act or any, rules made thereunder, otherwise than when required under law to attend personally, may attend in such proceedings by a person authorised by him in writing in this behalf, being a relative of, or a person regularly employed by, the aggrieved person, or an advocate who is entitled to plead in any Court of Law, or a Customs Consultant as defined and licensed under rules prescribed in this behalf, and not being disqualified under sub-section (2).
(2) No person who has been dismissed from Government service shall be qualified to represent a person under sub-section (1); and if any advocate or Customs Consultant is found guilty of misconduct in connection with any customs proceedings by the authority empowered to take disciplinary action against members of the profession to which he belongs, or if any other person is found guilty of such misconduct by the 3[Commissioner of Customs], the 3[Commissioner of Customs] may direct that he shall be thence forward disqualified to represent a person under sub-section (1) :
Provided that-
(a) no such direction shall be issued in respect of any person unless he is given a reasonable opportunity of being heard;
(b) any person against whom such direction is issued may, within one month from the date of receipt of the direction, appeal to the Board to have the direction cancelled; and
(c) no such direction shall take effect until one month from the date of receipt thereof by the person concerned or, when an appeal is preferred; until the disposal of the appeal.]

Authorized Representative: An authorized representative may appear on behalf of a person in customs proceedings, except when personal attendance is legally required.
Eligible representatives include relatives, regular employees, advocates, or licensed Customs Consultants, provided they are not disqualified by law.
Customs Authority: This entity includes any officer of customs, an appellate authority, the National Board of Revenue, or the Government, before whom a person may be required to attend in proceedings under the Customs Act 1969.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to investigate and determine misconduct by a person acting as an authorized representative and may issue a direction disqualifying them from future representation.
Any disqualification order issued by the Commissioner of Customs is subject to an appeal process to the National Board of Revenue and requires a prior opportunity for the affected person to be heard.
National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue acts as the appellate body for any person seeking to cancel a disqualification order issued by the Commissioner of Customs.
Person: Any person involved in customs proceedings has the right to be represented by an authorized person, provided the requirements of the Customs Act 1969 are met.
Persons dismissed from Government service are expressly prohibited from acting as authorized representatives.

member_objects.clause_title: Power to take sample of goods
member_objects.resolved_text:
199. Power to take sample of goods.- (1) The appropriate officer may, on the entry or clearance of any goods or at any time while such goods are being passed through the customs-area, take samples of such goods in the presence of the owner thereof or his agent, for examination or testing or for ascertaining the value thereof or for any other necessary purpose.

(2) After the purpose for which a sample was taken in carried out, such sample shall, if practicable, be restored to the owner, but if the owner fails to take delivery of the sample within one month of the date on which he is asked in writing to take its delivery, it may be disposed of in such manner as the 2[Commissioner of Customs] may direct.

(3) In the case of goods which consist of drugs or articles intended for consumption as food, and in respect of which the taking of samples for the purposes of this sub-section may have been authorised by a general or special order of the 3[Government], the appropriate officer may also in like circumstances take samples thereof for submission to, and examination by such officer of Government or of a local authority as may be specified in such order.

4[(4) The owner of any imported or exportable goods or his authorized representative may draw samples before presentation or transmission of bill of entry or bill of export thereof, as the case may be, subject to the conditions laid down by an officer of customs not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner.]

Appropriate Officer of Customs: The appropriate officer has the authority to collect samples of goods during their entry, clearance, or transit through the customs-area for the purposes of examination, testing, valuation, or other necessary official actions.
When collecting samples, the officer must ensure the presence of the owner or their agent.
In the case of food or drug items, the officer may collect samples for examination by specified government or local authority officials if authorized by a general or special government order.
Agent: The agent of the owner of the goods is required to be present when samples are being drawn by the appropriate officer of customs.
Goods: Samples of goods may be drawn for testing, examination, or valuation during the customs clearance process or while within the customs-area.
Once the purpose for testing or examination is fulfilled, samples should be returned to the owner if it is practicable to do so.
Commissioner of Customs: The Commissioner of Customs has the authority to direct the disposal of samples if the owner fails to collect them within one month of receiving a written request to do so.
Government: The government may issue general or special orders authorizing the collection of samples for food or drug products to be examined by specific authorities.
Imported or Exported Goods: Owners or their authorized representatives may request to draw samples of goods prior to the formal submission of a bill of entry or bill of export, provided they meet the conditions specified by a customs officer at or above the rank of Assistant Commissioner of Customs.
Authorized Representative: An authorized representative is permitted to draw samples of goods before the formal filing of entry or export documents under specific conditions established by an Assistant Commissioner of Customs or a higher-ranking officer.
Assistant Commissioner of Customs: An Assistant Commissioner of Customs or any officer of higher rank holds the authority to set the conditions under which an owner or authorized representative may draw samples of goods prior to the filing of a bill of entry or bill of export.
Bill of Entry: The owner or authorized representative may draw samples of imported goods before the presentation of the bill of entry, subject to compliance with conditions set by a senior customs officer.
Bill of Export: The owner or authorized representative may draw samples of export goods before the transmission of the bill of export, subject to compliance with conditions set by a senior customs officer.

member_objects.clause_title: Procedure for sale of goods and application of sale proceeds

Customs Goods Sale: The procedure for selling non-confiscated goods under this Act involves notifying the owner and selling the goods via public auction, tender, private offer, or other mutually agreed-upon methods.

The proceeds from the sale of goods must be distributed in a specific order: first to cover sale expenses, then to settle freight or other service charges, followed by payment of customs duties and taxes to the Government, and finally to pay custody charges to the relevant party.
Sale Proceeds Disbursement: Any remaining balance from the sale proceeds after all statutory debts, taxes, and service fees are paid is to be disbursed to the owner of the goods.
The owner of the goods is entitled to claim the balance of the sale proceeds, provided they submit an application within the prescribed time limit following the sale.
Government: The Government is entitled to receive payment for customs duties, taxes, and other dues incurred by the goods prior to the disbursement of any surplus funds to the owner.

member_objects.clause_title: Regulation of business of gold, etc
member_objects.resolved_text: 212. Regulation of business of gold, etc.- The 4[Government] may, by notification in the official Gazette, regulate business in, or connected with, gold or silver or precious stones or ornaments made of gold or silver or precious stones, within fifteen miles of the frontier or cost-line of 1[Bangladesh].

Government: The Government is empowered to regulate business activities concerning gold, silver, precious stones, or their ornaments within a specified distance from the frontier or coastline.
Trade of Gold and Precious Metals: Business activities involving gold, silver, precious stones, or ornaments made of these materials that occur within a specified distance from the frontier or coastline are subject to government regulation through official notification.

member_objects.clause_title: Protection of action taken under the Act
member_objects.resolved_text: 217. Protection of action taken under the Act.- No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against the 2[Government] or any public servant for anything which is done or intended to be done in good faith in pursuance of this Act or the rules.

Government: The Government is protected from any suit, prosecution, or legal proceeding for actions taken or intended to be taken in good faith under the provisions of the Customs Act 1969 or associated rules.
Customs Legal Proceedings: This clause provides legal immunity by restricting the filing of suits or prosecutions against the Government or public servants for actions performed in good faith pursuant to the Customs Act 1969 or its rules.
Customs Act 1969: This Act provides the legal foundation for the protection of actions taken by public servants and the Government when such actions are performed in good faith.
Rules: Actions taken in good faith under the authority of the rules made pursuant to the Customs Act 1969 are protected from legal proceedings.

member_objects.clause_title: Award of financial incentives to Customs Officers and employees
member_objects.resolved_text:
46[217B. Award of financial incentives to Customs Officers and employees - Notwithstanding anything contained to the contrary in this Act or any other law the Board may, in such manner and in such circumstances and to such extent as may be prescribed by rules, award an amount of the surplus collection of revenue at import stage as financial incentives to all Customs Officers and employees and officers and employees of the Board;

Provided that the collection of revenue at import stage for a given financial year exceeds the target of collection fixed by the Government for that financial year.]

National Board of Revenue: The Board is empowered to award financial incentives to customs and board personnel from surplus revenue collections at the import stage.
The manner, circumstances, and extent of these financial awards are subject to rules prescribed by the Board.
Customs Officer: Customs Officers are eligible to receive financial incentives derived from surplus import stage revenue collections, subject to conditions prescribed by rules.
Government Revenue Collection: Financial incentives for customs and board personnel are conditional upon the actual revenue collection at the import stage exceeding the target fixed by the Government for the relevant financial year.
Rules: These rules serve as the regulatory framework that governs the manner, circumstances, and extent under which financial incentives are awarded to customs and board employees.

member_objects.clause_title: Power to make rules
member_objects.resolved_text:
219. Power to make rules.- (1) The Board may, by notification in the official Gazette, make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act.
(2) Without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing provision, rules may be made on matters enumerated in the 1[Third Schedule].
(3) No rules relating to matters enumerated at items 19 and 22 of the 1[Third Schedule] shall be made without previous approval of the 2[Government] in writing.
(4) All rules made under this section shall, as soon as may be, be laid at the table of the 3[Parliament].
(5) All such rules for the time being in force shall be collected, arranged, and published at intervals not exceeding two years, and shall be sold to the public at a reasonable price.

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to issue rules through notification in the official Gazette to facilitate the implementation of the provisions of the Customs Act 1969.
The Board is responsible for collecting, arranging, and publishing all active rules every two years and ensuring they are made available for purchase by the public at a reasonable price.
Rules: Rules are subordinate instruments created to carry out the purposes of the Customs Act 1969 and must be laid before Parliament as soon as possible after their issuance.
Specific rules pertaining to matters listed under designated items in the Third Schedule require prior written approval from the Government before they can be enacted.
Third Schedule: The Third Schedule serves as the foundational list of matters for which the National Board of Revenue may prescribe rules.
Items numbered 19 and 22 within the Third Schedule are subject to a mandatory requirement of prior written approval from the Government before any related rules can be issued.
Government: The Government provides the necessary written approval required for the issuance of rules concerning specific sensitive matters identified in the Third Schedule.
Parliament: Parliament serves as the legislative body before which all rules created under the authority of this Act must be laid for oversight.

member_objects.clause_title: Removal of difficulties
member_objects.resolved_text: 222. Removal of difficulties.- If any difficulty arises in giving effect to the provisions of this Act, particularly in relation to the transition from the enactments repealed by this Act to the provisions of this Act the 1[Government] may, by general or special order made during the period of one year from the commencement of this Act direct such action to be taken as it considers necessary or expedient for the purpose of removing the difficulty.

Customs Act 1969: This clause provides the Government with the authority to resolve operational difficulties that may arise during the transition from previous legislation to the current Act.
The power to issue orders for the purpose of removing such difficulties is limited to a one-year period following the commencement of the Act.
Government: The Government is empowered to issue general or special orders to address and resolve any difficulties that arise while implementing the provisions of the Act.

member_objects.clause_title: Entrustment of functions of the customs officers to certain other officers
member_objects.resolved_text: 6. Entrustment of functions of the customs officers to certain other officers.- The Board may, by notification in the official Gazette, entrust, either conditionally or unconditionally, any functions of any officer of customs under this Act to any officer of the 8[Government].

National Board of Revenue: The National Board of Revenue is empowered to delegate the functions of customs officers to other government officers through a notification in the official Gazette.
The delegation of functions by the National Board of Revenue can be made either conditionally or unconditionally.
Officer of Customs: The functions of an officer of customs, as defined by the Customs Act 1969, may be entrusted to other officers serving the government.
Government: The officers of the government may be assigned to perform the functions of customs officers when authorized by the National Board of Revenue.

Officer of Customs: functions of an officer of customs

member_objects.clause_title: Exemption of certain classes of conveyance from certain provisions of this Chapter
member_objects.resolved_text:
59. Exemption of certain classes of conveyance from certain provisions of this Chapter.- (1) The provisions of sections 44, 52 and 54 shall not apply to a conveyance other than a vessel which carries no goods other than the baggage of its occupants.
(2) The 2[Government] may, by notification in the official Gazette, exempt conveyances belonging to Government or any foreign Government from all or any of the provisions of this Chapter.

Conveyance: Certain provisions of this chapter do not apply to conveyances, other than vessels, that are exclusively carrying the baggage of their occupants.

The Government has the authority to issue notifications in the official Gazette to exempt conveyances belonging to the Government or foreign Governments from all or specific provisions of this chapter.
Government: The Government is empowered to grant exemptions to government-owned or foreign government-owned conveyances from the provisions of this chapter through an official Gazette notification.
